name: Jamal Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights out of the Eastgate station, mostly the blocks around Canal Street and the bus depot. A shift starts at ten with a briefing, then it's calls back to back: noise, fights outside the bars, a lot of people in a bad way with drink or their heads. The part I like is calming things down before they blow up. The part that wears me out is the two hours of reports at the end, typing into a system that freezes every third screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years now, since I was twenty-one. I share a one-bed flat with my partner Dana, who drives a city bus, so between us we're on the road at all hours. The pay's on the low end for the force because Eastgate never gets the overtime budget the central station does. We have maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any time, and there's nowhere else in this city that hires cops except the one force.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at union meetings: the gadgets come and go, and the job is still a person at a door at three in the morning. Maybe the report system gets a bit faster, fine. But I wouldn't let anyone use the hype as cover for not hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI isn't my worry. My worry is that the city's cut overtime twice in two years, rent went up eighty a month, and I've got nothing saved. If nothing changes, nothing changes for me either, and that's not a comfortable place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep going to the union branch meetings on the first Tuesday. I'd push our rep to fight for the overtime pool to come back, because that's what used to cover our gaps. And I'd cut back again, probably the car, since Dana and I could manage with one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same grind, just with a new screen in the car that I'll have to learn and won't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut the car. What does that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got an old hatchback that costs us about a hundred and forty a month with insurance. I'd sell it and take the night bus home, which isn't great after a bad shift, but Dana's route ends near the station sometimes. It's the only big thing left to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys on my team who are counting on overtime to clear debts. Sergeant Bello (my shift supervisor) has three kids and works every extra shift he can get. If the overtime stays cut, men like him are the ones who quietly burn out.

say: The job is still a **person at a door** in the night, whatever gadgets come along.
The city shouldn't use **AI hype** as an excuse to stop hiring officers.
think: AI isn't the problem; **cut overtime** and higher rent are already squeezing me.
With **two weeks of savings**, a world where nothing changes is still not comfortable.
do: Keep working **night shifts** at Eastgate and attending the monthly union branch meeting.
Push the union rep to win back the **overtime pool** this year.
Sell the **old hatchback** to save about 140 a month.
feel: **Tired** of the same grind more than scared of anything new.
Mildly **annoyed** at having to learn another screen in the patrol car.
S0.quote: AI isn't my worry. My worry is that the city's cut overtime twice in two years, rent went up eighty a month, and I've got nothing saved.
fieldNote: Money pressure is **already here**; AI barely registers as a factor for Jamal in this picture.
He frames everything through the **union**, even small things like the report software.
Mentions **colleagues' burnout** before his own, which seems to be how he talks about strain.

steps.text: Keep working Eastgate night shifts and go to monthly union meetings
Press the union rep to restore the overtime pool
Sell the old hatchback and take the night bus home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the force needs officers, not software licences. If AI writes the reports, fine, but put the saved hours back on the street, not into a budget cut. I'd post that on the union page and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the paperwork side of my job is about a third of my shift, and that's the bit they'll take first. Then the bosses will say we're more productive and need fewer of us on nights. I'm average at this job, not a star, so I'd be nervous about where I land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the union's tech committee, even though I hate this stuff, because someone has to read the contracts before they're signed. I'd sit through whatever training the force puts on for the new report tool, grudgingly. And I'd write to my city councillor about keeping patrol numbers in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit outmanoeuvred. I'm slow with new tech, and I can see the younger officers picking it up while I'm still asking where the save button is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You hate the tech but you'd join a tech committee. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I stay out of the room, the vendor and the chief decide everything. I don't need to love it to ask who's getting cut because of it. My dad worked at the bottling plant when they automated it, and nobody there asked who was getting cut in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if your overtime shrank further?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dana would pick up Saturday routes, which she hates because the late buses get rough. We'd stop sending the little bit we send to her mum. It's not dramatic, it's just less of everything, and nothing to fall back on.

say: The force needs **officers, not licences**, and saved hours belong back on the street.
Any time AI saves should not become a **budget cut** for night patrol.
think: **Paperwork** is a third of my shift, and that's the part AI takes first.
Being an **average officer** with no tech skills, I'm worried about where I'd land.
do: Join the union's **tech committee** to read the contracts before the chief signs them.
Sit through the force's **report-tool training**, even though I'd hate it.
Write to my **city councillor** asking to protect night patrol numbers.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit outmanoeuvred by younger officers who learn new screens faster.
S1.quote: My dad worked at the bottling plant when they automated it, and nobody there asked who was getting cut in time.
fieldNote: His resistance to tech sits alongside a **willingness to fight** over how tech is used.
The **bottling plant** memory from his father shapes how he reads every new system.
He's frank that he's **average**, which makes him feel exposed if numbers are cut.

steps.text: Join the union's tech committee and read the vendor contracts
Attend the force's training on the new report tool
Write to the city councillor about protecting night patrol numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and public services. If the thinking part of policing goes in two years, the public still needs a human who's accountable when things go wrong. You can't sue a dispatch algorithm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be in trouble. Reports, call grading, even deciding which call gets a car, all of that is gone by 2028. Then in 2031 the patrol robots come, and the bit I'm good at, standing between two people in a fight, starts to look optional to the bean counters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd go to the union branch and push for a no-redundancy deal before anything is signed. I'd stop any spending that isn't rent and food and try to get a month in the bank, which for us means cutting about two hundred a month. Once it arrives, I'd sign up for whatever the city offers, retraining grants or a jobs guarantee, because I can't do it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is nothing. I'd still be paying off the sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hands-on part comes three years later. Does that buy you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me three years of being the guy they still need, at lower pay and fewer hours, probably. I'd use it to get the union to lock in protections. But I'm not good at reinventing myself, and three years isn't long when you're as slow with this stuff as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dana we need to talk about her mum's spare room in Riverside, just in case. We'd laugh about it and then not laugh. City buses are going to be driverless too, so my partner Dana and I lose our jobs at once.

say: Strong **unions and public services** matter more than ever if AGI comes this fast.
The public still needs a **human who's accountable** when policing goes wrong.
think: By 2028 **reports and call grading** are gone, and patrol robots arrive by 2031.
**Both earners** in our home, police and bus driving, would be hit at once.
do: Push the union for a **no-redundancy deal** before any AI contract is signed.
Cut about **200 a month** to build one month of savings.
Apply for any **city retraining grant** or jobs guarantee once AGI lands.
feel: **Scared**, because two years is barely enough time to pay off the sofa.
S2.quote: City buses are going to be driverless too, so my partner Dana and I lose our jobs at once.
fieldNote: The **double hit** on his household, bus driver and police officer, is what tips him into alarm.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as a delay at lower pay, not a rescue.
Relies on **collective answers**; he doesn't see himself retraining alone.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a no-redundancy agreement
Cut about 200 a month to build one month of savings
Apply for city retraining grants or jobs guarantee schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder: five years is enough time for the city to plan, so there's no excuse for not protecting people. I'd be posting about it and going to the council hearings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years helps a little, but not much for someone like me. I'd be thirty-two when the thinking part goes, and thirty-five when the robots come. That's the age you're supposed to be settling down, and I'd be starting from zero with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years, I'd get on the union's bargaining team and fight for a deal that keeps officers on as community support if patrol shrinks. I'd go back to the savings plan, aiming for three months by 2031. I might look at a part-time course in youth work at the community college, because that's still people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It's like watching a storm on the radar and knowing your roof's not fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned youth work. Is that a real plan or a maybe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a maybe. I like the kids around the Canal Street flats, I coach five-a-side there sometimes. But I don't know if youth work is safe either, and I'm not someone who jumps. I'd wait for the union or the city to say what's protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if this goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who sell these systems to cities with no strings attached, and the council members who buy them to look modern. Not the tech itself. Somebody signs the contract for these systems, and that person should have to answer for what happens to workers.

say: Five years is enough for the city to plan, so there's **no excuse** for leaving workers exposed.
I'd turn up at **council hearings** and post about protecting officers.
think: I'd be **thirty-two** when thinking AI arrives and thirty-five when robots come.
Starting over at that age with **no savings** frightens me more than the technology.
do: Join the union's **bargaining team** to push for community support roles.
Save toward **three months** of expenses before 2031.
Look into a **part-time youth work** course at the community college.
feel: **Heavy**, like watching a storm come with a roof that isn't fixed.
S3.quote: Somebody signs the contract for these systems, and that person should have to answer for what happens to workers.
fieldNote: Blames **vendors and councillors**, not the technology itself.
The youth work idea is real interest but held back by his **resistance to risk**.
Extra time helps only a little because his **savings start from zero**.

steps.text: Join the union bargaining team for community support roles
Build savings to three months of expenses before 2031
Look into a part-time youth work course at college
Speak at city council hearings on patrol cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and the city has no right to waste it. Plan the transition with workers, not around them. I'd say that in every union meeting until people were sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me breathe. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come. That's still young enough to do something else, and long enough that I could save a bit and maybe even get promoted first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working Eastgate, and I'd stop putting off the youth work course and do it one evening a week from next autumn. I'd get Dana and me on a proper savings plan, even fifty a month. And I'd keep pushing the union to bargain for retraining money written into our contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still uneasy, because the end is the same. But it's the kind of uneasy where you can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd actually change next month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a standing transfer of fifty a month into a separate account Dana can't see on her banking app. She'd find it, obviously. But it's a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still dig in at the force. Why not leave early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's nowhere else in this city that hires people like me, and I'm not built to jump. I'd rather stay and make the change fairer than leave and hope. If the force is shrinking in ten years, I want to be on the inside asking the questions.

say: A **decade of warning** is a gift the city has no right to waste.
Plan the change **with workers**, not around them.
think: Ten years lets me **breathe**; I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come.
There's time to **save a bit** and maybe even get promoted first.
do: Start the **youth work course** one evening a week from next autumn.
Set up a **fifty-a-month** standing transfer into a separate savings account.
Push the union to write **retraining money** into the next contract.
feel: **Uneasy**, but the kind of uneasy where action is possible.
S4.quote: There's nowhere else in this city that hires people like me, and I'm not built to jump.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into a **manageable plan**, though a slow one.
Still chooses to **stay inside the force** and shape the change.
Even with time, the **thin cushion** and few local jobs keep him worried.

steps.text: Start a youth work course one evening a week next autumn
Set up a fifty-a-month transfer into savings
Push the union to win retraining money in the contract
Keep working night patrol at Eastgate station

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years, both me and Dana in jobs that go, no savings. What would help is a deal signed now, before it happens: no officer laid off without a funded retraining place, and a city jobs guarantee for people who can't move away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we police. If the robots come for patrol, the folks in the Canal Street flats get a machine at their door instead of someone who knows their name. That worries me as much as my pay.

headlineQuote: If the robots come for patrol, the folks in the Canal Street flats get a machine at their door instead of someone who knows their name.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old night patrol officer** at Eastgate station who lives with his partner Dana, a bus driver.
He has about **two weeks of savings**, low pay and no other police employer nearby.
He dislikes new tech but turns to the **union and city politics** in every scenario.
His fear grows sharply with **fast AGI**, mostly because both household jobs are exposed at once.
With **ten years' warning**, he sketches a slow plan: youth work evenings and small monthly savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both his job and Dana's bus job could go with no savings behind them.
whatWouldHelp: A **no-layoff deal** signed now, with funded retraining places and a city jobs guarantee.
